gap: No result ChatGPT got puts the 4 kWh kits' headline numbers on one scale: Jackery's 6,000 cycles end at 70% capacity and EcoFlow's 4,000 at 80% (about 4,000 each at 80% on a straight-line fade), and the BLUETTI Elite 400's inverter is 2,600 W rated (3,900 W is 'Lifting Power') with a single 1,000 W, 12–60 V, 20 A solar input.
standout_why: I read five of the result pages: the three cited (PowerSized DELTA Pro 3 review, StormWatts 240V solar-input page, StormWatts bundle-vs-separate page) and two top StormWatts results (kits at the same panel watts, home-backup flagships). The flagships page already prints the raw cycle wordings side by side ('4,000 to 80%', '6,000 to 70%+', '3,000+') and the 240V page already gives per-port solar windows for the DELTA Pro 3 and F3800 Plus, so the raw material is there. What they lack: none converts the cycle claims to a common end point, and none of the five covers the Elite 400 or the ALLPOWERS R3500 at all (the 24-kit StormWatts table has neither). I did not open the other result pages (EnergySage, solargenreview, theoutageplan and others), so the gap claim holds only for the five read. Several maker pages returned HTTP 429, so the R3500 half of the table is missing and the EcoFlow cycle figure rests on rival pages.
decides: It confirms rather than changes the pick. On a common 80% end point the Jackery and EcoFlow cycle claims are a tie, so cycle life should not separate them. The Elite 400 kits are the lowest price per Wh in the size band ($0.46–0.61/Wh at link price) but are pre-orders (BLUETTI's page today: mid-January for orders placed on or after Nov 18), have the lowest rated AC of the group (2,600 W, under the 3,000 W bar ChatGPT set in its first answer) and ship with 35–70% of the station's 1,000 W solar cap. So they are the option for a shopper who can wait, not the pick. The ships-now kits we link in the band are the ALLPOWERS R3500 + SP037 400 W ($1,586.73 link, $1,803.10 store) and + SP039 600 W ($1,753.93 link, $1,993.10 store), but at 3,168 Wh they sit 20.8% under 4,000 Wh, right on the 'about 20%' line, and I could not open ALLPOWERS' page to normalise their cycle or solar specs. The EcoFlow DELTA Pro 3 kits ChatGPT priced at about $3,099 were out of stock on Nov 17 per PowerSized, and the Anker F3800 Plus page showed 'Sold Out' with no panel bundle today. The Anker SOLIX S5000 + 2× 400 W kit (5,024 Wh) is 25.6% over 4,000 Wh and falls outside the line.

findings.label: AC output as the maker states it: rated vs Lifting Power
findings.note: The page gives '2,600 W rated' and '3,900 W Lifting Power' and no separate surge figure in the text I read. The comparable continuous number against the DELTA Pro 3's 4,000 W and Jackery's 3,600 W is 2,600 W. Capacity on the page: 3,840 Wh.

findings.label: Solar input
findings.note: Page wording: 'Solar: 1,000 W Max., 12–60 V, 20 A Max.' Arithmetic: 1,000 W / 20 A = 50 V, so the array must operate at 50 V or more to reach the cap, within 10 V of the 60 V ceiling. The same line appears on the Elite 400+2*350W kit page (https://www.bluettipower.com/products/elite-400-2-350w, read 2026-11-18).

findings.note: Arithmetic at rated output: panel W / 1,000 W, and 3,840 Wh / panel W. Real output is lower. No Elite 400 kit we link fills the station's solar input.

BLUETTI's US product page gave no cycle figure in the text I read. Arithmetic on a straight-line fade: 3.84 kWh × 3,000 × 0.9 = about 10,400 kWh lifetime throughput to 80%.

findings.label: Cycle life with end point
findings.note: Read from the Jackery US store's search feed via storecheck; the product page itself returned HTTP 429. The wording is on the matching 3,584 Wh Battery Pack 3600 Plus listing; the HomePower 3600 Plus listing says only '6,000 cycles'. Normalised on a straight-line fade (my assumption, not a maker figure): 30 points of fade over 6,000 cycles means 80% is reached at about 4,000 cycles. Throughput to 80%: 3.584 kWh × 4,000 × 0.9 = about 12,900 kWh.

findings.label: Cycle life with end point (as rival pages print it)
findings.note: PowerSized's spec table reads '4,000 to 80%'; the StormWatts flagships page prints the same. EcoFlow's own page returned HTTP 429 today. Arithmetic: 4.096 kWh × 4,000 × 0.9 = about 14,700 kWh to 80%. Against Jackery's roughly 4,000 cycles at the same 80% point, the cycle counts tie; EcoFlow's higher total comes only from its larger battery.
